                        RESPONSE TO APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS TO
                        DIRECT TESTIMONY OF MIKE W. CORNETT

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
        COMES NOW, Mike W. Cornett (Cornett) to timely file this Response to
Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Mike W. Cornett (Interchange Item 4361)
and in support thereof respectfully show:

                                      I. Introduction

        Applicants do not object to Mr. Cornett offering expert scientific opinions — they
object to a landowner describing his own ranch. Mr. Cornett is the owner and operator of
Tenroc Ranch. He is permitted to testify about what he has built, what he observes on his
land, and how he expects a 765-kV transmission line to affect the property he has
managed for more than thirty years. Much of the testimony Applicants challenge is not
hearsay at all; the balance falls squarely within recognized exceptions for then-existing
state of mind, ancient documents, and lay opinion. The motion should be denied.
        Mr. Cornett's descriptions of his ranch — its condition, his improvements, his
daily operations, and what he observes there — are first-person factual narration based on
personal knowledge, not hearsay. 1 His statements describing the present state of the


1
    Tex. R. Evid. 602, 801.


                                           1 of 4
 ranch and his concerns about the proposed line reflect his then-existing condition and
state of mind, which fall within recognized hearsay exceptions.2 His opinions about visual
impact and operational disruption are admissible lay opinions rationally based on three
decades of direct experience. 3 The 1999 Angus Journal Land Stewardship Award — the
single document attached to Mr. Cornett's testimony that Applicants challenge as hearsay
(Interchange Item No. 4361) — is admissible as an ancient document. 4 The award itself is
also an operative fact: the recognition is what it is, not a statement offered for its truth.

                                           II. Argument

A. Mr. Cornett’s testimony is based on personal knowledge and constitutes
   permissible lay opinion
         A threshold point: much of the testimony Applicants challenge is not hearsay in
the first place. A landowner's first-person account of what he built, what he observes on
his property, and how he operates his business is factual narration based on personal
knowledge — not an out-of-court statement offered for its truth. 5 Mr. Cornett has owned
and operated Tenroc Ranch for over thirty years. His testimony about the ranch's
condition, the improvements he has made, the daily operations he conducts, and the
anticipated impacts of the proposed transmission line rests on direct observation and
personal experience. To the extent any of these descriptions touch on the present state of
the property, they are independently admissible as statements of then-existing condition
and state of mind. 6
        To the extent Applicants challenge any of Mr. Cornett's observations about how
the proposed line will appear on the ranch as improper opinion, those observations are
admissible under Rule 701. A lay witness may offer opinion testimony rationally based on
his perception and helpful to determining a fact in issue.7 Mr. Cornett's observations flow
from three decades of managing this property — they are not technical predictions
requiring expert qualification.

B. Mr. Cornett’s statements regarding his opposition and concerns are admissible
   state of mind
       Mr. Cornett's expressions of concern about the proposed routing, his opposition
to Links E7 and E12, and his intentions regarding continued use of the ranch constitute

 admissible statements of then-existing state of mind and intent. Statements concerning a
declarant's then-existing state of mind, including future intent or plan, fall within the
hearsay exception.8 These statements are offered to establish Mr. Cornett's actual mental
state and reasons for opposing specific routing alternatives, not to prove the truth of
external facts.

C. The 1999 Angus Journal article is admissible under multiple hearsay exceptions
       The Angus Journal article from October 1999 is admissible as an ancient
document. Rule 803(16) excepts from the hearsay rule statements in a document that was
prepared before January 1, 1998, or that is at least twenty years old, the authenticity of
which is established. 9 The article is more than twenty-five years old and predates this
controversy by decades. Its authenticity is established because it is a published article
from the Angus Journal — the national industry publication of the American Angus
Association — not an internal document susceptible to fabrication. 10 Beyond the hearsay
exception, the award itself is an operative fact, not a statement offered for its truth: the
publication of the article is the recognition. The fact that Tenroc Ranch received the 1999
Land Stewardship Award is established by the existence of the article, regardless of what
any sentence inside it asserts.

                                           III. Conclusion

        For the foregoing reasons, Intervenor Mike W. Cornett respectfully requests that
the Administrative Law Judges overrule Applicants' objections to his direct testimony in
their entirety, including the objection identified in Applicants' Exhibit A to the 1999
Angus Journal Land Stewardship Award (Interchange Item No. 4361), and admit the
testimony and accompanying exhibit as an ancient document under Tex. R. Evid. 803(16),
or in the alternative as an operative fact establishing the recognition itself.
